red.focus: Understand duties recorded in early public judgments
red.summary: Begin with the obligations that ancient legal texts placed on buyers, sellers, household members and people causing harm. Learn that the duties of an ancient society differed according to status and institutional power.
checklist: I can identify an obligation in an early legal text
I can distinguish a contractual promise from a public penalty
I can connect duties with their historical social setting

sections.title: Duties Make Expectations Visible
sections.body_md: Hammurabi's collection includes provisions concerning exchange, property, wages and household relationships. These examples show how a legal order could specify consequences when people failed to perform expected conduct. A farmer, trader or builder might face duties defined by the ruler's legal framework. Yet these were not modern universally equal contract rules. Their effect depended on the person's role and social position, and the form of proof or sanction prescribed by the judgment. Studying them teaches that law organizes expectations before a wrong happens.

sections.title: The Meaning of an Obligation
sections.body_md: A duty says that an identified person ought, under an applicable rule, to do something or refrain from doing it. A private obligation may require delivery of goods or repayment; a public prohibition may forbid conduct and attach a penalty. Ancient sources sometimes combined these ideas in forms unlike modern categories. A historian should avoid calling every ancient transaction a contract as we understand it today. The safer method is to state who owed what, to whom, under which legal source, and with what consequence.

sections.title: Duties Reflect Social Design
sections.body_md: A rule about a builder's responsibility, a debtor's payment or a household obligation communicates more than individual morality. It reveals what the governing order sought to protect: trade, property, hierarchy, family organization or public security. The same text may protect one person's interest while reinforcing another person's subordination. Early legal duties thus teach a double lesson. Law coordinates human activity and makes promises predictable, yet the content of legal obligation must still be judged against justice and the people it affects.

yellow.focus: Trace Roman obligations and legal categories
yellow.summary: Study how Roman jurists refined obligations involving agreement, wrongdoing and transfer of value. See why modern private-law vocabulary owes much to Roman classification without treating Roman doctrine as identical to current law.
checklist: I can distinguish obligations arising from agreements and wrongs
I can explain the role of Roman juristic classification
I can identify the limits of historical analogy

sections.title: An Obligation Links Persons
sections.body_md: Roman legal thought developed sophisticated ways to explain why one person owed performance to another. Jurists described obligations arising in connection with contracts and delicts, among other sources. This vocabulary helped organize different claims and remedies. It did not mean that all persons could contract on identical terms or that every present legal category existed unchanged. The important intellectual move was to treat obligation as a legal relationship that could be analyzed separately from ownership or political authority.

The important intellectual move was to treat obligation as a legal relationship that could be analyzed separately from ownership or political authority.

sections.title: From Transactions to Doctrine
sections.body_md: A sale or loan can generate duties between people; a wrong causing legally recognized harm can generate a duty to answer for it. Roman lawyers distinguished these kinds of legal relationships and explored what actions the claimant could bring. Their answers depended on historical procedure and social status. Studying these origins makes current legal categories easier to question: when a modern text uses the word contract, does it identify a genuine consensual duty, or has the jurisdiction assigned liability through another rule?

sections.title: Transmission Without Identity
sections.body_md: Roman concepts influenced medieval scholarly learning and later European codification. But reception involved translation, selection and adaptation rather than copying the past intact. A term may survive while its social setting, legal remedy or definition changes. The historical lawyer compares the old and new rule's source, beneficiaries, elements and enforcement. This approach avoids two opposite errors: assuming modern private law was invented without precedent and assuming it is merely Roman law under different names.

orange.focus: Compare feudal obligations with emerging private-law duties
orange.summary: Examine a world where land tenure, personal allegiance and customary service intertwined. Distinguish duties created by social rank from obligations increasingly framed through general private-law concepts.
checklist: I can explain duties linked to feudal tenure
I can compare customary service with contractual exchange
I can recognize changing forms of legal obligation

sections.title: Land and Service Were Entangled
sections.body_md: In many medieval European arrangements, landholding could bring obligations of service, payments and loyalty within a hierarchical political order. Such duties were not always freely negotiated like modern commercial promises. Their legal meaning depended on status, tenure, local custom and the institutions enforcing them. A historian should avoid presenting feudalism as a single uniform code across Europe. The more accurate question is which relationship the particular source described and what recognized duties followed from it.

The more accurate question is which relationship the particular source described and what recognized duties followed from it.

sections.title: Promises Become Legal Problems
sections.body_md: As trade, towns and royal courts developed, questions about agreements, debt and commercial assurance acquired new institutional forms. Customary practices, canon law, revived Roman learning and local procedures influenced different legal systems. Not every promise was enforceable in the same way. An analytical comparison asks whether the duty rested on tenure, oath, exchange, religious obligation or an actionable form of agreement. The point is not that modern contract law suddenly replaced feudal duty, but that sources of obligation diversified and their relative importance changed.

sections.title: Who Could Demand Performance?
sections.body_md: Legal duties have a human dimension: who was entitled to demand performance and which forum could enforce that demand? A lord, tenant, merchant or ecclesiastical institution might possess different legal powers. Some relationships involved coercion and social dependence rather than meaningful bargaining equality. This history matters when modern law appeals to consent as the justification for obligation. A lawyer should ask whether a formally voluntary undertaking was made under conditions in which refusal was genuinely possible.

black.focus: Critique the historical expansion of legal duty and social responsibility
black.summary: Trace how modern legal systems came to recognize obligations beyond a narrow bargain or individual wrong. Evaluate the relation between industrial risk, the welfare state and duties to people who cannot effectively negotiate their protection.
checklist: I can analyze why industrialization challenged older duty categories
I can distinguish contractual freedom from actual bargaining power
I can defend duties that protect vulnerable parties without arbitrary overreach

sections.title: Industrial Change Exposed New Risks
sections.body_md: Factories, railways and mass markets created recurring harms that could exceed traditional bilateral bargains. Workers, passengers and consumers might face danger without meaningful control over the enterprise causing it. Legal systems developed varied responses through labor regulation, accident compensation, negligence, insurance and social security. These reforms did not occur everywhere at the same speed, nor did they eliminate private responsibility. Their shared historical question is whether duty should depend only on a personal promise when social organization creates predictable risks for strangers.

Their shared historical question is whether duty should depend only on a personal promise when social organization creates predictable risks for strangers.

sections.title: Freedom to Agree Is Uneven
sections.body_md: Classical private-law accounts often emphasize autonomy: people are bound because they chose an agreement. Yet consent may be constrained by poverty, monopoly, dependency or unequal information. Consumer-protection and employment laws in many jurisdictions respond through nonwaivable duties and minimum standards. Such laws may protect dignity but can also raise practical costs or limit choices. A doctoral comparison distinguishes the moral ideal of genuine consent from the institutional conditions under which it is claimed.

sections.title: A Theory of Duty for the Present
sections.body_md: Modern problems such as platform work, algorithmic decision systems and environmental harm cross familiar boundaries among contract, tort and public regulation. A credible reform proposal should identify who controls the risk, who benefits, who can prevent injury, and which institution can enforce a duty proportionately. The historical lesson is not that duties always become broader. It is that changing social facts can expose an outdated allocation of responsibility, requiring explicit reasons for keeping or revising the rule.
